newsitem.title: USA: Accused U.S. broker test-taker pleads guilty.
newsitem.headline: Accused U.S. broker test-taker pleads guilty.

text.p: A stockbroker accused of taking tests for other brokers as part of a huge Wall Street licensing scam pleaded guilty on Wednesday to criminal charges and will serve up to six years in prison, prosecutors said.
Igor Shekhtman, 36, of Encino, California, was accused of taking 28 tests for 17 brokers in Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia, Wisconsin and New York.

Charged with 152 counts of forgery and facing up to 196 years in prison, he admitted in a plea bargain with the Manhattan district attorney's office to two counts of forgery and criminal possession of a forged instrument.
He will be sentenced to two to six years and ordered to pay a $30,000 fine on May 29, prosecutors said.
On Monday, another accused test-taker, Robert Idzi, of Pleasantville, New York, pleaded guilty to forgery. He faces up to six years in prison and a $20,000 fine when he is sentenced on April 28.
Idzi was originally charged in a 108-count indictment with taking 20 separate tests for 15 brokers in eight states.
Also this week, three of 53 stockbrokers who allegedly sent Idzi and Shekhtman to take their six-hour tests pleaded guilty to forgery, and a fourth man pleaded guilty last week.
The tests were administered by the National Association of Securities Dealers (NASD).

Last month, 30 of the brokers struck a plea bargain with prosecutors to avoid prison and were ordered to pay fines of up to $20,000. They also agreed to lifetime bans from the NASD and are prohibited from trading in New York state.
Most of the people charged in the scandal worked at 17 small and medium-size brokerage firms, including Stratton Oakmont, Hanover Sterling & Co. and Gruntal & Co.
